units.title: Computing digital roots
units.description: Repeat the digit sum until one digit remains.
learningObjectives: Compute the digital root of any number
Predict digital roots of large numbers quickly

blocks.text: Take a number, add its digits, then add the digits of the result, and keep going. Every number eventually settles onto a single digit — its **digital root**.

content.text: The digital root of 94,567 is 4. One more round of digit-adding always finishes the job, since the digit sum of any number under 100 is under 18.

blocks.text: The digital root equals the remainder on division by 9 — except that a remainder of 0 shows up as the digit 9. Digital roots are therefore always between 1 and 9.
Since only remainders modulo 9 matter, you can cast out 9s while adding. Better still: the digital root of a sum or product can be found from the digital roots of the parts.

blocks.value: dr(a + b) = dr\big(dr(a) + dr(b)\big), \qquad dr(a \times b) = dr\big(dr(a) \times dr(b)\big)

blocks.question: What is the digital root of 987,654?
blocks.explanation: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 39, and 3 + 9 = 12, 1 + 2 = 3. The digital root is 3 — and indeed 987,654 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 9.

units.title: Digital roots and divisibility
units.description: Use digital roots to test divisibility by 9 and 3 and to verify sums.
learningObjectives: Detect multiples of 9 by a digital root of 9

blocks.text: A digital root of 9 means the number is a multiple of 9. A digital root of 3 or 6 means divisible by 3 but not by 9. That makes digital roots a fast divisibility and error-checking tool.

content.text: Riya added 4,218 + 5,907 and wrote 101,125. Check with digital roots:
The answer's digital root should be 9, but it is 1 — Riya made an error. The correct sum is 10,125, whose digital root is 9 ✓.

blocks.text: dr(a + b) must equal dr(dr(a) + dr(b)). If the check fails, the calculation contains an error.

Digital roots catch most mistakes — digit swaps, wrong digits, dropped digits — but not all. Two errors that shift remainders by equal amounts cancel out, and errors that are multiples of 9 are invisible. A passing check is strong evidence, not proof.

blocks.question: A student computes 7,342 + 2,885 = 10,227. Does the digital-root check pass?

options.text: Yes — both sides have digital root 9
Yes — both sides have digital root 7
No — the left side gives 9 and the right side gives 3
No — the check needs products, not sums

units.title: Digital root puzzles
units.description: Find missing digits and mystery multiples using digital roots.
learningObjectives: Determine missing digits from digital-root constraints
List numbers with a given digital root

blocks.text: If a number must be divisible by 9, its digital root must be 9 — this pins down missing digits beautifully.

blocks.title: Worked example: which digit hides in 34★2?

content.text: 34★2 must be divisible by 9, so its digit sum must be a multiple of 9.
For 9 + ★ to be a multiple of 9 with ★ a digit 0–9, ★ = 0 or ★ = 9. Both 34,002 and 34,092 are divisible by 9.

blocks.text: Digital-root constraints often leave a small set of digit candidates — list them, then apply any extra conditions (even, largest, smallest) to finish.

Every digital root selects a family: digital root 7 numbers are 7, 16, 25, 34, 43, … stepping by 9 each time. Puzzle clue *'my digital root is 7 and I am a two-digit even number'* gives 16, 34, 52, 70, 88 — five candidates.

blocks.question: A two-digit number has digital root 2 and is odd. Which of these could it be?
blocks.explanation: The digital-root-2 family is 2, 11, 20, 29, 38, 47, … Among the options only 29 is in the family and odd: 20 and 38 are even, and 45 has digital root 9.
